title: Do Richer Countries Actually Work Less?

segments.label: scene 1 (title)
segments.text: Depending on where you live in the world, a full year on the job can look radically, almost shockingly, different.

segments.label: scene 2 (statement)
segments.text: In Sudan, the average worker logged 2,658 hours in 2023, making it the highest recorded workload among all 124 nations.

segments.label: scene 3 (world_map)
segments.text: At the opposite extreme sits Germany, where workers logged just 1,335 hours in 2023, the lowest overall.

segments.label: scene 4 (slope)
segments.text: Across developed and developing economies, annual hours have shifted dramatically over the past several decades.

segments.label: scene 5 (compare)
segments.text: In the United States, workers put in 1,789 hours in 2023, which is a 7% decline since 1970.

segments.label: scene 6 (line)
segments.text: Across the Atlantic, United Kingdom workers logged 1,523 hours in 2023, dropping 12% over that same span.

segments.label: scene 7 (scatter)
segments.text: These striking global contrasts bring us to a fundamental question: do richer countries actually work less?

segments.label: scene 8 (world_map)
segments.text: According to Our World in Data, mapping annual working schedules across continents reveals striking regional patterns. High workloads cluster heavily in specific parts of the world.

segments.label: scene 9 (countries_bars)
segments.text: In Central Africa, workers in Congo log 2,534 hours per year. Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates averages 2,514 hours annually.

segments.label: scene 10 (countries_bars)
segments.text: Jordan follows closely with 2,483 annual hours per worker, while Pakistan logs 2,471 hours.

segments.label: scene 11 (slope)
segments.text: In East Asia, long working schedules remain prominent. South Korea logs 1,910 hours per year, whereas workers in Japan average 1,654 hours.

segments.label: scene 12 (compare)
segments.text: Looking across the ocean to Latin America, workers in Mexico record 1,629 hours a year.

segments.label: scene 13 (line)
segments.text: By contrast, Northern European nations sit near the bottom. Denmark averages 1,380 hours, Norway stands at 1,412, and Sweden logs 1,432.

segments.label: scene 14 (statement)
segments.text: Intriguingly, Yemen also ranks among the lowest at 1,382 hours. Geography alone clearly does not tell the whole story.

segments.label: scene 15 (line)
segments.text: Historically, rapid development reshaped national labor patterns. Back in 1970, South Korea's bustling workforce logged a staggering 2,919 hours per worker.

segments.label: scene 16 (compare)
segments.text: As industrialization matured and living standards rose, South Korea recorded a massive 35% reduction in annual working time through 2023.

segments.label: scene 17 (gauge)
segments.text: Japan experienced a comparable shift. Workers there logged 2,185 hours annually in 1970 during its postwar economic boom.

segments.label: scene 18 (bars)
segments.text: By 2023, Japan's annual workload had fallen by 24% as services grew and labor laws adapted.

segments.label: scene 19 (slope)
segments.text: Western Europe saw dramatic reductions as well. Germany stood at 1,972 hours per year in 1970, subsequently dropping by 32%.

segments.label: scene 20 (statement)
segments.text: Rising productivity and modern labor policies systematically allowed advanced economies to turn wealth into leisure.

segments.label: scene 21 (multiline)
segments.text: Across these major industrialized nations, the overall trajectory over the last half-century points toward shorter working lives.

segments.label: scene 22 (statement)
segments.text: What is driving this steady decline in annual working hours across advanced economies? Higher productivity plays a fundamental role.

segments.label: scene 23 (multiline)
segments.text: As technology and automation boost hourly efficiency, workers can produce identical output in significantly fewer hours.

segments.label: scene 24 (statement)
segments.text: Statutory vacation expansion also reshaped schedules. Governments across Western Europe codified mandatory paid time off and strict overtime caps into national law.

segments.label: scene 25 (line)
segments.text: France offers a clear example. In 1970, average French workers logged 1,993 hours per year, falling to 1,487 by 2023.

segments.label: scene 26 (counter)
segments.text: That transformation marks a 25% reduction in annual workload, driven by legal workweek limits and generous holiday policies.

segments.label: scene 27 (line)
segments.text: The United Kingdom experienced a similar shift. British workers logged 1,733 hours in 1970 before labor reforms reshaped the modern schedule.

segments.label: scene 28 (multiline)
segments.text: Ultimately, rising national prosperity allowed developed countries to convert economic efficiency into more free time for workers.

segments.label: scene 29 (scatter)
segments.text: So, does wealth actually buy leisure time? Mapping 126 nations reveals a clear, inverse relationship.

segments.label: scene 30 (statement)
segments.text: As national GDP per person rises, hours worked tend to fall. This correlation sits at -0.40.

segments.label: scene 31 (kpi)
segments.text: Take the United States. With a GDP per person of $74,352, workers log 1,789 hours annually.

segments.label: scene 32 (line)
segments.text: Compare that to Germany. Their GDP per person is $63,140, yet workers put in just 1,335 hours.

segments.label: scene 33 (counter)
segments.text: Meanwhile, Mexico maintains a different balance. At $21,865 per person, the annual workload is 1,629 hours.

segments.label: scene 34 (line)
segments.text: South Korea illustrates how this evolves. Despite a GDP per person of $54,029, its historical intensity persists at 1,910 hours.

segments.label: scene 35 (multiline)
segments.text: Ultimately, the data shows that while wealth enables shorter hours, institutional norms define the actual pace of life.

segments.label: scene 36 (line)
segments.text: In the United States, annual work hours have finally stabilized. After decades of change, the trend has flattened out.

segments.label: scene 37 (gauge)
segments.text: Since 1970, the average American worker has seen a total reduction of 7% in their annual workload.

segments.label: scene 38 (statement)
segments.text: This shift isn't just an American story. Across high-income nations, annual hours have reached a new, consistent baseline.

segments.label: scene 39 (race)
segments.text: The data suggests that the push for shorter hours is now a structural feature of modern, developed economies.

segments.label: scene 40 (multiline)
segments.text: While individual paths differ, the era of rapidly declining work hours has transitioned into a period of stability.
